To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the competitive mechanism is informationally most efficient under one characterization of informational efficiency, but not under another.

(1) the informational size of a message space can be measured in at least two ways, one of which is more appealing than the other; (2) the competitive mechanism, when applied to an arbitrary message space, is not necessarily the most efficient allocation procedure according to either of these measures; (3) however, when the message space is a “simple” one, the competitive mechanism, applied to it, is the most efficient allocation mechanism according to both of the measures.
the competitive mechanism is informationally most efficient under a characterization of informational efficiency which, in a sense, is the most natural.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the informational efficiency of mechanisms for allocating resources.
a generalization of a result by Mount and Reiter, and with a comparison of alternative characterizations of the notion of informational size.
the informational efficiency of various mechanisms for allocating resources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the competitive mechanism is informationally most efficient in the sense of being informationally most efficient.
the competitive mechanism is the “informationally best” procedure for allocating scarce resources.
the competitive mechanism is informationally optimal under the best characterization of informational efficiency.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the competitive mechanism is the most efficient mechanism for allocating resources in the presence of private information, if and only if the information is “perfect” (in the sense of Mount and Reiter) and the information is “complete” (in the same sense).
the competitive mechanism is not informationally most efficient for allocating resources.
the notion of informational size is a useful tool in characterizing and comparing mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of additional structure, the informational efficiency of a mechanism is not an absolute property of the mechanism, but is relative to a characterization of informational efficiency.
the notion of “informationally most efﬁcient” procedure is not well deﬁned without further assumptions about the nature of the problem.
there is no single “correct” characterization of informational efficiency.
